note: Rabbi Yitzhak asked Rav Nahman why he had not come to the synagogue to pray. Rav Nahman said he was too weak. Rabbi Yitzhak suggested he gather ten men at home to pray; Rav Nahman said that would be too much of a burden on them. Then let the congregation send a messenger to tell you when they are praying, Rabbi Yitzhak said, so you can pray at the same moment. When Rav Nahman asked why he was going to such lengths, Rabbi Yitzhak quoted Rabbi Yohanan in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai: the 'time of favor' in the Psalm is the time when the congregation prays.
why: The Gemara has been quoting Rabbi Yohanan's teachings in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai; this exchange introduces another of them, and other Sages then add their own verses showing the special power of praying with a community.

people.name: Rabbi Yitzhak
people.about: A Sage of the Land of Israel who urges Rav Nahman to pray together with the congregation.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: A leading Babylonian Sage and judge, here too weak to come to synagogue.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The leading Sage of the Land of Israel in the third century, quoted by Rabbi Yitzhak.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: A great second-century Sage, student of Rabbi Akiva, whose teaching Rabbi Yohanan passes on.

terms.meaning: A prayer quorum, called a minyan: the ten adult men needed for communal prayer.
A phrase from Psalms 69:14, read here as a moment when God is especially ready to accept prayer.

note: Mar, son of Ravina, held a wedding feast for his son and saw that the Sages there were getting too merry. He brought out a precious cup worth four hundred zuz and smashed it in front of them, and they grew sad.
why: The Gemara is discussing whether excessive joy is proper; it has just told of Sages rebuked for being too joyful, and follows this with Rav Ashi breaking a glass at his own son's wedding and a mournful song sung at Mar's feast.

people.name: Mar, son of Ravina
people.about: A Babylonian Sage who sobered his son's wedding guests by breaking an expensive cup.

terms.meaning: A silver coin; four hundred zuz was a very large sum.

note: Rav Pappa visited the home of Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan. After the meal was over, something more to eat was brought in, and Rav Pappa took it and ate without saying a new blessing. His hosts asked whether he did not hold that once a meal is finished one may not eat again without a blessing. He answered that the rule, correctly stated, speaks of the table being 'removed', not of the meal being finished.
why: The Gemara is working out when a meal counts as over, so that further food needs its own blessing; right after, Rava and Rabbi Zeira argue the same question at the Exilarch's house, using Rav Pappa's 'removed' wording.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: A Babylonian Sage and head of an academy, a visitor here.

people.name: Rav Huna, son of Rav Natan
people.about: A Babylonian Sage, the host of the meal.

terms.meaning: In Talmudic times each diner ate at a small table that was carried away when the meal ended. Taking it away, not just stopping eating, marks the meal's end.
